rv.q: This is dazzling ensemble theater, partnering Blanchett with the sly and thrilling Richard Roxburgh, her Vanya in 2012.

Weaving together these characters and their hollow lives in a context that connects them both to Chekhov's Russia and to our own uncertain world, Upton, Crowley and this accomplished company have elevated a problematic play into something unexpectedly satisfying.
Blanchett and Roxburgh give off so much heat that it’s hard to focus on all these secondary moths.
The play itself is a more fitfully successful affair.
Blanchett has the movie-star charisma that makes you want to know at all times what she's thinking, and the stage transparency that provides the information at a glance.
“The Present” is also a terrific vehicle for its two stars, Cate Blanchett (Mr. Upton’s wife) and Richard Roxburgh.
That leaves a lot of messy stuff to tie up in the post-intermission acts, and they’re not as much fun.
But here Ms. Blanchett’s take-charge inventiveness is as sorely taxed as that of her character.

This crass, seriocomic script lumbers along for three palpable hours, alternately tedious and odious, expecting us to care about its petty, miserable, bed-hopping Russian characters without giving them witty or touching things to say.
Her presence in The Present makes it an instant event on Broadway; but the play and production are more than worthy, thank you very much.
Blanchett and Roxburgh are electrifying...A well-paced three hours to be savored for the fine performances and interesting hints of themes to come.
At turns acidly satirical and starkly astute, The Present illuminates the gravity-free existence that built Russia today.
The brilliance of Crowley’s production lies in its ability to peel back the layers of its many characters to reveal relatable and laughable flaws.
Happily, the Sydney Theatre Company put a contemporary spin on the 19th Century manuscript, turning Chekhov's flawed tragicomedy into a masterful production.
Tonally, the lightning shifts from humor to pathos to profundity in this scene is the register of the production as a whole, and sometimes that can be discombobulating.

"The double-Oscar-winning star is just one shining jewel in a mostly dazzling show full of farcical humor, heartbreaking pathos, and pointed political observation. Clocking in at three hours, the comedy-drama does have its slow points—the third of four long acts is especially lead-footed.
Without the two mighty bright stars — who, like the whole cast, are making Broadway debuts — it’d be a slow-starting, fitfully amusing and longwinded evening at the Barrymore Theatre.
Along with the gun and the bomb, the flaws of this great, sprawling, messy play are not entirely obliterated by the stellar performances and direction.

Indeed, the rare chance to see this excellent all-Australian ensemble on stage, led by Oscar winner Blanchett and the blazingly charismatic Richard Roxburgh (as the self-important, womanizing Mikhail Platonov), shouldn’t be missed.
It's harder to sense the misgivings underneath Mikhail's bluff exterior.
As hard as it tries, The Present never really makes the case for why Chekhov’s forgotten play should be remembered alongside his more famous ones.

"Upton's 'The Present' is a mixed blessing. On the one hand, it brings the team of Cate Blanchett and Richard Roxburgh to New York for their Broadway debuts, and reintroduces theatergoers to a fairly unknown play by Anton Chekhov.
These people want to blow up their world, and in a way they do, most entertainingly.
It is an attention-grabbing moment in Blanchett’s Broadway debut performance – and one of the show’s few unmitigated pleasures.
John Crowley's carefully calibrated production takes its time – it runs to a hefty three hours – but rewards the attention.
For all its strengths, Upton and Crowley have taken their adaptation too far.
Like previous adapters, Upton has not succeeded in turning Chekhov's messy draft into a play.
As directed by John Crowley with a spare visual design, “The Present” is an uneven, uneventful and aimless mess.
The play is so bad it seem to be in an unknown language.
Upton and director John Crowley shape and sharpen the material into a slowly percolating, soul-tugging, and brightly sparkling tour-de-force.
Watching her is seeing a legend at work in her heyday.
Add to this the fact that the play could have been cut by another hour, and you have a fairly unsatisfactory evening.
Blanchet and Roxburgh are electrifying, however Roxburgh nor the role of Platonov carry the burden of being a male sex symbol.
But no amount of fog can mask the stretches of dullness in the three-hour production.

Despite the fine production values and outstanding performances by Blanchett and Roxburgh, three hours of this muddled, interminable tragicomedy is not much more than a first draft of Chekhov's later well-formed theatrical visions of Russian society.
'The Present' leaves the audience enthralled and satisfied through the dynamic portrayals by Ms. Blanchett, Mr. Roxburgh and the excellence of the supporting cast.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Chekhov adaptation, with Cate Blanchett's magnetic Broadway debut and Richard Roxburgh's performance widely praised, but the three-hour runtime and unwieldy source material proving divisive.

vs.sum: The Ethel Barrymore Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and minimal obstructions, though some box seats have limited views. Sound quality is average, with some reports of less than ideal acoustics. Comfort is typical for a Broadway theater, with decent legroom in some areas. However, facilities are lacking, with only one restroom on the lower level leading to potential congestion.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
